title: A contact path for an architecture studio
metaTitle: A contact path for an architecture studio
excerpt: Tell a future client what happens after they write, how soon you reply, and what to have ready. The action is a project conversation. Ten fields will lose them.
alt: Pale blue and orange ink swirls on a white ground, two colors meeting in a single field the way a first note and a reply have to meet.
caption: Two colors finding an edge. A first message needs a clear edge too. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should we ask for on the first message?
faqs.answer: A name, an email, the address or listing, and a few sentences on the use. Whether they own the site is worth a single question. A budget band is optional. A ten-field form that asks how they heard of you, their company size, and a file upload will lose the client who was ready to talk.

faqs.question: How fast should the page promise a reply?
faqs.answer: Promise the window you already keep. Write it in working days, and mean it. A slower true reply is better than a same-day line you miss when the office is on site. Say what the reply contains: whether you can take the project, and what the first conversation is for.

faqs.question: Should the first meeting produce a sketch?
faqs.answer: Say no on the page if the first meeting is for fit. Clients who expect a free scheme will be disappointed in a way that sours the job. The page can say the conversation is to hear the site and to decide whether to propose a first stage. Drawings come after that agreement.

markdown:
An architecture studio contact page should tell a client judging taste before competence what happens after they reach out, how soon, and what to have ready. The action is to start a project conversation. A form with ten fields is a way to lose them.

They have already seen the work. They do not need a second brochure here. They need the terms of the first reply, in sentences a busy person can use.

## What happens after they write

Say the sequence in the order they will feel it. They send a note. You read it. You reply with a yes, a no, or a request for one missing fact. If it is a yes, you propose a conversation or a first-stage fee. If it is a no, you say so plainly. That sequence is the product of this page.

Write it as three sentences above the form, not as a help-center article below it. People who are ready will not scroll through a policy to learn whether anyone is there. [Google's helpful content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether a reader leaves able to take the next step. The next step here is to send the right note, with a clear picture of the reply.

Name the purpose of the first conversation. Fit. The site, the use, and whether this office is the right one. Not a concept design. Not a quote for an unseen slope. When the page is quiet about purpose, clients invent one, and the invented one is usually "they will sketch something."

Say who replies. "Ada reads new projects" is more reassuring than "the team." A client judging taste has picked you for the work. They want to know a person stands at the door. If several people share the inbox, say that the project lead replies, not a rotating marketing alias with no name.

If you are closed to new work, say that on this page before the form. A disabled button with a date you will reopen is kinder than a form that falls into a void. Update the sentence when it changes. A stale "we are booked until spring" in autumn is a small lie that careful clients notice.

## How soon, in your own words

Publish a reply window you will keep on a week when two people are on site. Two working days is a common honest window. Some offices do better. Use yours. Do not borrow a speed from a studio whose marketing you admire. A missed promise does more harm than a slower true one.

Define the window. "We reply within two working days to say whether we can take a first conversation." That is different from "we reply within two working days with a fee proposal." The second promise needs a site you have understood. Do not make it unless you mean it.

Mention holidays and the weeks you are on site installs only if they truly stop the inbox. A single line in those weeks is enough. The rest of the year, the standing sentence should be visible without a banner.

Auto-replies are fine if they repeat the window and the human still writes. An auto-reply that says "your enquiry is important" and then nothing else is the ten-field form in disguise. If you use one, make it specific: we have the address, we will write by Thursday, we do not need another email unless the closing date changed.

Track the promise for a month before you print a faster one. If the true median is three days, the page should say three. The client can plan. You can keep your word.

## What they should have ready

Ask for the smallest set that lets you judge fit. Name, email, address or listing link, and a short note on use. Add one question if you need it: do you own the property, or are you deciding whether to buy?

A budget sense can be a single optional line. Some clients have a builder's number. Some have a life and no number yet. Forcing a budget dropdown with ranges you invented will produce fiction. The pricing page, if you have one, already showed the shape of the fee. Point to it. Do not make them re-derive it in a form.

Do not ask for a full brief, a survey, or a mood board on the first message. Offer a way to attach a file if they have one, and do not require it. Required uploads are where phone users abandon you.

Spell the list on the page so they can gather it before they tap. A client standing in a house they might buy should know that the listing link is enough for a first note. They can send photographs later.

Here is a sufficient form:

- Name
- Email
- Address or listing
- What the project is, in a few sentences
- Whether they own it

Five lines. The last can be a yes or no. Everything else can wait for the conversation you just promised.

## A form people can finish

[The W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) organizes accessibility under perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A contact form fails all four when labels are missing, the button is tiny, errors are a red border with no words, or the page only works for one browser's autofill. Labels should be visible text, not placeholders that vanish. Errors should say which field and what to do. The button should say "Start a project," matching the rest of the site.

Make the form work on a phone, because that is where the decision often happens. The email field should invoke an email keyboard. The address can be a normal text field. Do not use a map widget as the only way to give you a location. Maps fail, and they are slower than a sentence.

Confirm the send on the same page. "We have it. We will reply within two working days." Repeat the window. Offer a copy by email if you can do it simply. Do not dump them on a blank thank-you screen with a newsletter pitch.

Keep a plain email address visible as well, for people who will not use a form. Publish the address you actually read. If projects and press should go to different places, say so in one line each. Two addresses with labels. Not a grid of departments.

Test the path by sending a note from a phone that is not logged into your office tools. Read the reply you get, including the auto-reply. If you are confused, the client was too.

## Ten fields is how you lose the project

The long form feels responsible inside the office. It asks for company, role, timeline, budget, source, square meters, and a PDF. Each field was added after one awkward call. Together they tax the careful client who already trusts the work and is busy.

Cut back to the list above. You can ask the rest on the call, when the answer can be a sentence instead of a dropdown. The page's job is to start a project conversation, not to complete your CRM.

Watch for other losses on the same screen. A captcha that fails twice. A required phone number. A demand that they pick a service from a list of twelve metaphors. A privacy essay above the button. Link the privacy note. Do not make it the content.

If you are unsure which fields your last ten clients actually needed, read those threads. Circle the facts that changed your reply. Those are the fields. The rest were curiosity.

When the path is muddled and you want to settle it before a rebuild, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the current form and one recent enquiry that went well. The half hour should decide the promise, the fields, and the sentence above the button. Hanabi designs and builds the page after that. The copy has to be yours, because only you can keep the reply window.

## The same door on every page

The contact page is the long version. The path itself should show up on the homepage, on a project, and beside the people, with the same label. A client who decides next to a photograph should not have to remember a clever word hidden under Studio.

Write one block you can reuse. One sentence on the promise. The short list of what to send. The button. Place that block at the end of a project page. Keep the full form in one location so you do not maintain five forms that drift. If a project template ends with "download the monograph," replace that ask. A PDF can live with the credits. It is not the conversation.

Say which project they were viewing if the note starts there. A hidden field with the project name is enough. You should not ask them to retype a title they can see. You should be able to tell, in the inbox, whether they wrote from the lane house or from the people page.

Read the block out loud on a phone. The promise has to be on screen with the button. A sticky bar that covers the last field is a broken door. Send one test from a project page and one from the contact page. Both should arrive where a person actually looks, with the reply window you published.

If the office uses a shared inbox, write down who checks it on site days. The page can be perfect and still fail when the mail sits until Monday and the promise said two days. The path includes the habit. The habit is not a plugin.

## What the rest of the site should stop doing

A clear path still fails if the pages around it perform taste and hide the work. A fullscreen render with no words will feed this form with the wrong people, and it will fail to feed it with the right ones. The contact page cannot rescue a site that never showed a decision.

The cut list is [what not to put on the site for an architecture studio](/blog/what-not-to-put-on-the-site-for-an-architecture-studio). Read it with the form open. Anything that delays the building, the constraint, or this conversation is a candidate to leave off.
